item.title: @omarsar0：Meta研究人员提出Benchmark Factory方案：通过智能体循环将内部代码变更转化为编程评测基准
item.description:
Interesting paper from Meta showing how to build coding evals from your own codebase.

(bookmark it)

Good benchmarks are hard to create, but using this method with agents looks promising.

They propose Benchmark Factory, an agent loop that turns merged internal code changes into benchmarks. It writes the query that selects tasks, runs models of known relative strength, and repairs the benchmark until it passes a set of quality checks. These checks need no per-task human labels.

To make sure the checks catch bad benchmarks, the authors fed them bad benchmarks on purpose. A benchmark that was far too easy got rejected. So did benchmarks with five different kinds of broken grading. When they scrambled which model was which, a bad benchmark slipped through at most 1.4% of the time.

On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus 4.7 at high effort above low effort (60.6% vs 54.4%) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs 60.5%). 9 of 10 per-team comparisons agreed.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18890

Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/benchmark-factory-agentic-benchmark-creation-via-dataset-curation-and-label-free-2611.18890

In February 2026, QUBT completed its acquisition of Luminar Semiconductor, including Freedom Photonics in Santa Barbara. That added semiconductor lasers, optical amplifiers, detectors and photonic packaging.

item.title: @convequity：硅光子光学开关与机械开关在损耗及端口数上面临不同技术取舍
item.description:
Silicon-photonics optical switches can change paths in nanoseconds, but they lose light at every stage, and that loss can make them hard to deploy.

An optical circuit switch keeps the signal as light from end to end. $LITE's MEMS mirrors and HUBER+SUHNER's piezoelectric Polatis do this mechanically, switching in milliseconds.

Electro-optic silicon-photonics switches route light through paths on a chip and reconfigure in nanoseconds. That could let a network rearrange connections as traffic changes.

The problem is insertion loss, and it comes from keeping the light on a chip. Light loses power at the couplers where it enters and leaves the chip, along the waveguides that carry it across, and at each switching element. A switch with more ports usually needs more stages in series, and each stage leaves less power for the next, so less reaches the receiver.

Mechanical switches lose far less. A MEMS mirror or a Polatis piezoelectric actuator steers the beam through free space from the input fibre to the output fibre in one pass, with no chain of on-chip stages, so the loss stays low even at large port counts.

Amplifiers can make up the loss on the chip, as an IBM-led demonstration showed. They cannot recover data already corrupted by noise.

Our view: the switch types will coexist. We expect the choice to depend on how often a network changes its connections, port count, optical loss and cost.

Deeper dive available at Convequity.

item.description:
KB Securities sees DRAM contract prices up 40% next year. NAND average selling prices rise 30% on a contract basis.

Spot prices fell over the past month. DRAM dropped 5% and NAND fell 20%. Contract prices kept rising. The gap between spot and contract widened to more than 20% in November. Spot tracks weak smartphone and PC sales. It misses the server DRAM and enterprise SSD demand that drives earnings at Samsung and SK Hynix.

Global DRAM demand is projected to grow 25% in 2027. Supply grows 18%. Server DRAM demand rises 56%. Major customers are expected to receive only about 70% of the DRAM volumes they need. That shortfall pushes contract prices higher.

Global NAND demand grows 19%, roughly matching supply. PC and smartphone NAND slows. Enterprise SSD demand rises 54% and stays short. Enterprise SSDs make up more than 65% of NAND revenue at Samsung and SK Hynix. At SanDisk and Kioxia the share is 30-40%. Consumer weakness has a smaller effect on the Korean makers’ average selling prices.

Recent stock drops mixed Nvidia leadership changes with US policy concerns and falling spot prices. Contract prices that set the two companies’ profits remain solid.

How much of the 40% DRAM contract rise holds if server customers still receive only 70% of ordered volume through 2027?

@nicbstme：I never looked at the X algorithm before today. It's open source, and they have a file called param .rs with the actual weights used to rank your “For You feed”

The most surprising thing: copying a post's link has a weight of 20. Liking it has a weight of 0.7. Copying the link is the most valuable thing you can do with a post, weighted almost 30x more than a like and 4x more than a reply.

My guess why: when you copy a link, you're about to paste it somewhere else. A group chat, Slack, an email. That's the strongest signal there is that a post is worth something, and it brings new people onto X. A like costs nothing. Sending something to a friend means you're putting your name on it.

The rest of the list tells a bit of a similar story like a reply is 5, a quote is 5, sharing by DM is 5, following the author is 4, a share is 2.1, a repost is 1, and a like is 0.7. Literally I didn’t know that repost does almost nothing.

The negatives are brutal btw a report is -234, a mute is -59, "not interested" is -53 and a block is -31.

A reply from someone you follow who follows you back gets a 15x boost. Conversations between real connections matter most (and not bots!)

Reposts don't reach strangers. A filter drops a repost for anyone who doesn't follow the reposter. A quote is a new post, so it can travel much further. Quote beats repost so you always have to add your own thoughts to a post.

item.title: @omarsar0：麻省理工学院与英伟达推出QDA智能体技术优化大语言模型量化设计
item.description:
Great paper from MIT and NVIDIA.

I think this is an important step toward personalized, accessible RSI.

The best recipe changes with every model and precision, so experts usually redesign it by hand. QDA hands that loop to an agent that builds and tests candidates over many rounds.

They show that QDA beats the strongest public recipes by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 points at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search.

Evaluation speed is what makes this work. Scoring one quantized reasoning model normally takes tens of GPU-hours. QDA scores each candidate in minutes by measuring its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces the agent never sees. Promising candidates then get long generations to catch repetition loops.

A shared library of public PTQ methods lets the agent combine them without porting each codebase by hand.

On the 320B MoE GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, QDA recovered 98.3% of FP8 accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every checkpoint runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23388

@isidoremiller：For a while I have been obsessed with the idea that there is a fundamental difference between "context" as we have grown to understand it and "knowledge", which is what we actually prize and desire and what translates into real-world outcomes.

It's become clear to me that as the volume and scope of work delegated to AI grows, legacy systems of context management will not be able to scale cleanly, no matter how much we try to use AI to speed things up. In domains that are not pure code, it is an asymmetric race where the slop generators are always outpacing the context curators. There is no way to break this formation.

Unless you shift your perspective and move up a plane. Legacy static context bootstraps synthesized knowledge. Knowledge grows organically and dynamically with rich environmental feedback. It becomes "real" in a sense that legacy context is often not and so can be evaluated and verified and improved and maintained in a truly autonomous and scalable fashion.

Data teams and curators do not lose control in this vision of the world; they develop increased leverage, their signal-to-noise ratio improves, and everyone (and their agents) coalesces around the outcomes that matter —knowledge— instead of intermediate busywork.

item.title: @convequity：分析称Lumentum与Coherent面临来自多方竞争激光器稀缺性或难持续
item.description:
Lumentum ($LITE) and Coherent ($COHR) have pricing power because lasers are scarce. In our view that scarcity may not last, because competition is coming from four sides.

First, shared lasers. With optical amplifiers, one laser can feed several channels, and designers can add amplification where it is needed instead of relying on one high-power laser. That could mean fewer lasers sold per unit of bandwidth, or less demand for the highest-power products. The second risk falls mainly on Lumentum, because ultra-high-power CW lasers are now its core business.

Second, new architectures for short links. MicroVCSEL designs spread bandwidth across many small, slower lasers. MicroLEDs go further and replace lasers altogether in suitable applications.

Third, LiDAR companies are bringing their laser and amplifier know-how into data centres. Aeva ($AEVA) announced an amplifier with reported output above 630 mW and a joint development agreement for a major hyperscaler's deployment. MicroVision ($MVIS) introduced an external laser module for co-packaged optics and says it is in talks with potential licensees and development partners.

Fourth, making standard 100 mW CW lasers is fairly commoditized know-how, and many companies are trying to scale up production, including Semtech ($SMTC), Sivers, Nokia ($NOK) and MACOM ($MTSI).

Total optical revenue at both incumbents could still grow as networks expand. The risk is that customers gain more ways to obtain the light they need, which would weaken the pricing power that comes from scarce lasers.

item.title: @convequity：AI集群构建商正重新设计光链路以减少稀缺激光器依赖并降低成本
item.description:
AI cluster builders are redesigning optical links so they need fewer scarce lasers. Feeding eight channels from one laser is one way to do that.

Silicon is good at carrying and modulating light but poor at emitting it. So today's 1.6 Tbit/s transceivers depend on indium phosphide (InP) lasers, and the highest-power ones are expensive, difficult to manufacture and in short supply. A customer that relies on them cannot deploy faster than those lasers become available.

That gives customers a strong reason to change the design. One route separates two jobs: a continuous-wave (CW) laser supplies steady light and a silicon-photonics modulator encodes the data, which widens the choice of laser suppliers. Other routes are lower-power lasers embedded in the system, and microLED links that replace lasers in suitable applications.

Another route is sharing one laser, using semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs), chips that use electrical power to boost light. Our own illustration, not a disclosed product: one CW seed laser is split into four branches, four SOAs boost the light, and each branch is split again to feed two channels. That gives eight 200 Gbit/s channels from one seed laser plus four SOAs instead of eight lasers.

An ideal eight-way split leaves each channel one-eighth of the power, a loss of roughly 9 dB. The SOAs make up that loss, so the power does not all have to come from one high-power laser.

This is not eight times cheaper. SOAs use electricity, add manufacturing and integration cost, and add some noise. Splitting also works only when every channel uses the same wavelength.

item.description:
LiDAR developers have spent years solving three problems that data-centre optics now face, and in our view $AEVA's photonics platform and wavelength expertise are among the closest fits for the optical-connectivity applications we are considering.

The three problems are powerful lasers, many lasers packed densely into one compact package, and receivers that recover faint returning light in a noisy environment.

As optics move into co-packaged and near-packaged designs, more channels must fit in a small package, and several can share one laser. Sharing one laser across several channels requires a strong source and often amplification, which is where Aeva's products fit.

Wavelength matters because each band needs a different light-emitting semiconductor (the gain material that generates and amplifies the light), plus matching optics and receivers. You can't just retune a laser for a new band, so Aeva's indium phosphide (InP) platform gives it an edge over LiDAR peers working in other bands.

We also rank Aeva highly on readiness because it has already launched the business and a customer project. In August 2026 it announced an optical-connectivity business and a joint development agreement with an unnamed optical-engine provider for a major hyperscaler's deployment. Aeva targets initial deployment in the second half of 2027 and a production ramp in 2028.
